name: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen

lead: Zinc oxide is a mineral sunscreen filter that covers UVA and UVB. It is one of two filters the FDA considers generally recognized as safe and effective.
Its appearance on the skin is the usual complaint, which is why nanoscale versions exist.

paras: Particles on the skin absorb UV light and also reflect and scatter some of it.
Studies of nanoparticle zinc oxide on human skin found very low penetration. Laboratory work has examined zinc release under UV and combinations with organic filters.

lead: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen uses zinc oxide, an inorganic (mineral) compound, as its active ultraviolet filter. Zinc oxide protects against both UVA and UVB light and, with titanium dioxide, is one of the two mineral filters used in sunscreens.[1]

Wikipedia describes it as the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber approved by the US FDA for sunscreen and as photostable.[2] As of 2021 zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were the only sunscreen filters the FDA categorized as generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE).[1]

Much published research concerns nanoparticulate zinc oxide, which is used to avoid the white appearance of conventional mineral products. Studies using skin-penetration assays and in vivo microscopy have examined whether the particles pass through human skin.[3][4]

paras: Wikipedia states that mineral filters work mainly by absorbing UV light, with some reflection and scattering.[1] Early-2000s research cited there suggested zinc oxide performed better than titanium dioxide at 340 to 380 nm in the UVA range.[1]

Mineral sunscreens can leave a visible white cast, which the sunscreen article says some consumers dislike and which may lead some to apply them more thinly.[1] Nanoscale zinc oxide does not scatter visible light as strongly, so products look less white.[2] A patent family describes powder blends of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide with defined size distributions for sunscreens.
In the US, labels do not need to disclose whether mineral ingredients are nanoparticles, while the EU requires disclosure.[1]

A 2007 in vitro study using Franz diffusion cells and electron microscopy on human epidermis found that less than 0.03 percent of the applied zinc from a micronized zinc oxide formulation penetrated.[3] A 2020 review of ten years of in vivo multiphoton microscopy work on human skin concluded that it had been used to assess whether nanoparticulate zinc oxide penetrates, in a period when a precautionary approach to nanoparticles in consumer products was being argued.[4]

A 2010 laboratory study reported that UVB irradiation could release zinc ions from commercial zinc oxide sunscreen and examined the effect of zinc accumulation on cultured human keratinocytes.[5] Wikipedia notes that some zinc is slightly absorbed into skin, and describes zinc oxide as non-toxic in sunscreen use, with fumes from industrial heating a separate hazard.[2] Wikipedia also mentions a case in which combinations of zinc oxide and small-molecule organic absorbers showed photodegradation and toxicity in zebrafish embryos.[2]

No clinical trials of zinc oxide sunscreen on appearance outcomes were found. Human skin-penetration studies exist: an in vitro study on excised human epidermis and in vivo multiphoton microscopy studies.[3][4]

timeline.event: In vitro study reports under 0.03% penetration of a micronized zinc oxide formulation.[3]
FDA lists zinc oxide and titanium dioxide as the only GRASE sunscreen filters.[1]
